title: Streaming vs Batched Fallback Topology & SLA Review - Cormorant Tech
summary: SE-led deep dive on p95/p99 behavior during streaming fallbacks, multi-hop network effects, KV cache hit patterns and batching/quantization tradeoffs; agreed to run cross-region microbenchmarks and share quantization evals.
transcript:
Header: 2026-04-14 15:30 UTC | Duration: 58m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Evelyn Park (Cormorant CTO), Marco Ruiz (Platform Eng), Sofia Klein (SRE)

-- Auto-summary (generated, may be noisy):
Maya: run benchmarks, share security doc. Jordan: explained streaming fallback topology and KV cache behavior. Customer asked about p99 when cross-region fallback occurs and options to mitigate.

00:00:05 Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to focus this session on the observed p95/p99 spikes when y'all see the streaming fallback kick in, and how topology and caching interact. is that still what you're seeing evelyn?
00:00:18 Evelyn Park: yeah, uh hi, thanks. yeah the spikes map to when your hosted node in eu-west failsover and traffic goes to us-east. p50 is fine but p99 jumps a lot, like, 300-500ms.
00:00:34 Jordan Patel: thanks, that matches what we often see when there's an extra network hop. quick context — streaming adds per-token flushes so there's slightly different packet patterns than non-streaming. when you add a cross-region hop it compounds.
00:00:50 Marco Ruiz: can you quantify? we need numbers for SLA tradeoffs. our goal is p95 < 120ms and p99 < 350ms for our chat feature.
00:01:04 Jordan Patel: in our lab runs, with EU->US hop + streaming enabled, median ~45ms, p95 ~140ms, p99 ~420ms. non-streaming (single response) with same path had p99 ~260ms. so streaming increases the tail because of additional round trips and Nagle/packetization effects.
00:01:30 Sofia Klein: we saw weird jitter even within same region though — sometimes p99 > 300ms without cross-region. is that KV cache related?
00:01:40 Jordan Patel: could be. couple of things: KV cache hit rate, hotkey concentrations, and async cache refill times after model variant swaps. when a key misses we may fetch full KV from disk or remote store and that can add 100-300ms depending on topology.
00:01:58 Evelyn Park: we use prefix caching for session tokens, but we do see hotkeys for top 10k users. is there a recommended approach?
00:02:10 Jordan Patel: we recommend split TTLs and sharded keyspace — avoid single global hotspot. prefix/KV cache is per-serving-pool, so if traffic rebalances to a single pool you'll see more misses. also warm-up on rollout helps.
00:02:27 Maya Chen: quick note — we'll put our suggested cache sharding doc in the slack thread after this call.
00:02:35 Marco Ruiz: about fallbacks — how does the routing decide to send to another model variant vs another region? we'd like to prefer same-region quantized variant before cross-region full model.
00:02:46 Jordan Patel: routing policy is configurable. you can set 'prefer-region' and 'compatible-variants' priority. for your use case, policy that prefers a local quantized variant (int8/4bit) over cross-region fp16 gives better tail behavior in practice, with a small accuracy tradeoff.
00:03:06 Sofia Klein: what accuracy tradeoff are we talking about? our evaluation set is sensitive — we can't lose more than ~1.5% F1 on our rerank tasks.
00:03:18 Jordan Patel: int8 end-to-end varied, but a targeted quantization profile we ran with your sample prompts showed approx 1.1% median delta on our eval suite. 4-bit aggressive quantization had up to 3% delta on some edge-case prompts. we'll share the eval artifacts.
00:03:36 Evelyn Park: shareable please. and run them with our prompt set.
00:03:40 Maya Chen: noted. next steps item.

00:06:12 Jordan Patel: deeper on streaming: when streaming we flush partial token frames every 80-120ms typically; that means more small packets and more sensitivity to TCP push and proxy buffering. with some LBs/NAT gateways you get added serialization delays. non-streaming bundles tokens server-side and returns a single response, which hides intermittent network jitter but increases median.
00:06:35 Marco Ruiz: so it's a trade: streaming better UX perceived latency but worse p99 sometimes?
00:06:43 Jordan Patel: exactly. streaming reduces time-to-first-byte for long responses — perceived latency — but p99 for completion can be worse if network path is unstable. For your SLAs, we can do adaptive streaming: start streaming locally then if hops increase, switch to chunked non-streaming.

00:09:50 Sofia Klein: curious about kernel cold starts. we had tail events when a model version rotated and GPU kernels warmed up. saw 600-900ms spikes. any mitigations?
00:10:02 Jordan Patel: yes kernel cold start is real — when a new model or quantization profile loads, JIT/compilation and kernel selection can add hundreds of ms. mitigation: keep a warm pool or pre-load the quantized variant into a standby GPU. we support model pre-warm hooks and background prefetch.
00:10:22 Evelyn Park: costs escalate if we keep warm pools though. need a cost analysis.
00:10:27 Maya Chen: Random note: Redwood Optimize has a config that suggests warm pool sizing based on traffic percentiles; we'll include an estimate.

00:14:10 Marco Ruiz: let's talk KV cache coherence — when we have multi-region read-through caches how do invalidations propagate? we saw stale tokens and re-fetch storms when TTL expired simultaneously.
00:14:23 Jordan Patel: invalidate-on-write vs. time-based TTL — we default to TTL for performance, but you can enable async invalidation via pub/sub across regions. downside is extra metadata traffic. Another pattern: jitter TTLs to avoid thundering herd which seems applicable here.
00:14:43 Sofia Klein: what's a safe jitter?
00:14:46 Jordan Patel: typically 5-15% jitter over TTL window; for 30s TTL use +/- 3-5s randomization.

00:18:05 Evelyn Park: networking specifics — how many additional hops do you see in your hosted path? and where are the TLS terminations?
00:18:17 Jordan Patel: hosted: edge LB -> regional gateway -> serving plane -> model worker. TLS is terminated at the edge LB then re-established to the gateway; we can also do passthrough if you need end-to-end TLS for private deployments. each hop adds ~2-5ms on average in-region, cross-region adds ~40-80ms depending on fiber and peering.
00:18:42 Marco Ruiz: the extra TLS re-establishment is heavy?
00:18:46 Jordan Patel: the handshake cost is usually amortized across long-lived connections. but if your clients are short-lived HTTP connections, it matters. Using HTTP/2 keepalives or our connection pooling reduces that.

00:22:03 Sofia Klein: can we run a microbenchmark where we induce a forced region-failover and capture p50/p95/p99 across streaming/non-streaming with local quantized variant preference?
00:22:13 Maya Chen: yes that's doable. we'll run with your workload profile and include three axes: streaming on, streaming off, streaming adaptive; and routing policy set to prefer-local-quantized vs prefer-low-latency-region.
00:22:27 Evelyn Park: timeline? we want results before vendor selection review in two weeks.
00:22:32 Maya Chen: we'll aim for 7 business days.

00:25:10 Jordan Patel: small note on batching: larger batch sizes give much better throughput (tokens/sec), but increase tail latency especially for short prompt workloads; batching is best when request arrival variance is low and you can tolerate added dispatch latency. For your mixed profile we recommended dynamic batching with latency SLO guardrails — e.g., max wait 30ms or max batch 8.
00:25:33 Marco Ruiz: show us numbers please — what does that do to p95/p99?
00:25:37 Jordan Patel: example: with max_wait 30ms and max_batch 8 we saw ~25% token cost reduction and p95 increase of ~10-15ms, p99 increase ~40-60ms for short prompts. if you bump max_wait to 80ms, p95 improves cost but p99 gets worse.

00:28:55 Evelyn Park: re: quantization, will runtime fallback to higher-precision if quality regression is detected? we need safe-guarding.
00:29:05 Jordan Patel: yes, Redwood supports redlines: automatic quality checks tied to prompt sets. if a quantized variant crosses configured threshold, routing can failover to higher-precision locally or send to hosted fallback. This can be async or immediate depending on policy.
00:29:23 Sofia Klein: ok that helps. we need the rollback window to be small.

00:33:11 Marco Ruiz: procurement/ops quibble — private deployment inside our VPC: how does that change the topology and tail characteristics?
00:33:22 Jordan Patel: private deployments remove cross-cloud hops and eliminate our edge-to-region TLS break, so typical tail reduction is 30-60ms p99 improvement vs hosted cross-region fallbacks. But you take on intra-datacenter network management and we provide tooling to minimize KV replication lag.
00:33:43 Evelyn Park: if we do on-prem, can we still use Redwood Console for traces?
00:33:48 Maya Chen: yes, the private control plane can push telemetry to your account with RBAC. for air-gapped we offer a collector that writes to a local store you host.

00:37:02 Jordan Patel: specific mitigation playbook we recommend for your case:
- prefer-local-quantized routing policy
- enable adaptive streaming that downgrades to chunked responses on cross-region detection
- configure KV TTL jitter and 5-10 warm standby workers per pool
- dynamic batching with max_wait 30ms and max_batch 8
- pre-warm quantized kernels for expected traffic peaks

00:37:40 Marco Ruiz: cost estimate on those mitigations?
00:37:44 Maya Chen: we'll include a cost delta for warm pool vs on-demand and for private vs hosted. ballpark: warm pool adds ~12-18% infra cost for the reserve capacity needed to keep p99 within your SLA for peak windows.

00:40:20 Evelyn Park: security question — if we prefer local quantized variant, does the model artifact live in our VPC or yours?
00:40:27 Jordan Patel: for hosted, model weights are in our managed storage but we can enable customer-managed keys (KMS) and encryption at rest. For private deployments model artifacts live in your environment per agreement.

00:42:55 Sofia Klein: about telemetry — we need token-level latency breakdown. the Console shows token-level but sometimes it's noisy. can you correlate network hop traces to model worker time?
00:43:05 Jordan Patel: yes we have distributed tracing headers and per-hop timing; we'll run an instrumented run with diag-level traces and provide a small parsing script you can use.

00:46:38 Marco Ruiz: any known incompatibilities with our infra — we use a custom NAT/egress egress proxy.
00:46:46 Jordan Patel: proxies that buffer small packets (like certain older NGX configs) can be problematic for streaming. config tweaks — disable proxy buffering for the route, increase http2 keepalive — generally resolves it. we'll share a checklist.

00:50:00 Evelyn Park: can you summarize the remediation steps and next actions?
00:50:07 Maya Chen: sure. recap: 1) Redwood runs microbenchmark in 7 business days with your prompts and induced region-failover, comparing streaming/non-streaming/adaptive + local quantized routing. 2) Jordan provides quantization eval artifacts using your prompt set. 3) Maya shares cost delta and warm-pool recommendation. 4) Jordan shares KV sharding + TTL jitter checklist and proxy buffering checklist. 5) we set follow-up check-in after results to decide pilot.

00:50:35 Evelyn Park: thanks, let's try to get the benchmark early if possible.
00:50:39 Maya Chen: we'll aim to do it in 5 biz days if our infra slot frees up; otherwise 7 days.
00:50:45 Marco Ruiz: tight timeline but doable.

00:55:12 Jordan Patel: action items are on the call — i'll also include a sample CI job to run model quantization regression checks automatically.
00:55:27 Sofia Klein: ideal.
00:57:00 Maya Chen: final — i'll drop the next steps and links in email and create a follow-up calendar for the results review. appreciate the time.
00:57:10 Evelyn Park: thanks all.
00:57:20 (end)
